lesson.title: Fatty Acids: A Polar Head Dragging a Nonpolar Tail
lesson.summary: Fatty acids are long hydrocarbon chains capped with a carboxyl group, and that combination of a water avoiding tail and a reactive acidic head makes them the basic building block from which triglycerides and phospholipids are constructed.
lesson.body:
A fatty acid has a deceptively simple structure: a long, unbranched chain of carbon atoms, typically somewhere between four and thirty six carbons long though most biologically common ones run from fourteen to twenty, with a carboxyl functional group (-COOH) at one end. That carboxyl group is the acid part of the name, since it can donate a hydrogen ion and behave as a weak acid in solution, and it is also the reactive end of the molecule, the site where a fatty acid links to glycerol through a condensation reaction to build a triglyceride or a phospholipid. Everywhere else along the chain, carbon is bonded almost exclusively to hydrogen and to neighboring carbons, which is what makes the tail of a fatty acid so intensely nonpolar and hydrophobic, in sharp contrast to the small polar carboxyl head.

That structural split, a polar acidic head attached to a long nonpolar tail, is the same basic architecture that will reappear when you study phospholipids, and it is worth noticing here first because fatty acids are the simplest molecule where it shows up clearly. On their own, free fatty acids are only mildly soluble in water, oriented with their heads dissolved and their tails pushed together to minimize contact with water molecules, a preview of the self assembly behavior that becomes essential once fatty acids are incorporated into membrane lipids.

Biochemists sort fatty acids first by chain length and then, more importantly, by how many carbon to carbon double bonds sit within that chain, a distinction covered in full in the next section on saturated and unsaturated fats. A few specific fatty acids are worth naming because they show up constantly in nutrition and biochemistry. Palmitic acid, a sixteen carbon chain with no double bonds, is one of the most common saturated fatty acids in both plants and animals. Oleic acid, an eighteen carbon chain with a single double bond, is the dominant fatty acid in olive oil. Linoleic acid, an eighteen carbon chain with two double bonds, and alpha-linolenic acid, an eighteen carbon chain with three double bonds, belong to the omega-6 and omega-3 families respectively, named for the position of the double bond closest to the tail end of the chain rather than the carboxyl end.

Linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid share another label: they are essential fatty acids, meaning the human body lacks the enzymes needed to insert double bonds at those particular carbon positions and so must obtain them directly from food. This is a useful reminder that not every biomolecule an organism needs is one it can synthesize from scratch; some structural details, in this case exactly where along a carbon chain a double bond sits, are locked in by which enzymes an organism's genome happens to encode.

Fatty acids rarely exist as free floating molecules inside cells for long. Instead they are almost always found condensed onto a glycerol backbone, either singly or doubly in a phospholipid or triply in a triglyceride, or occasionally attached to other molecules such as cholesterol. Understanding the fatty acid on its own, its carboxyl head, its variable length, and its variable number of double bonds, is the foundation for understanding every one of the larger lipid classes built around it.
